title: The dead ox
translation: Someone told this story: "A man was selling an ox. The buyer said he'd bring the money the next day and collect the ox then. During the night, the ox died. So the buyer came out ahead, and the seller lost."

A man sitting nearby heard it and said, "The owner did lose, true. But he also gained a great deal. Here's why. Living things don't know how close death is. The ox didn't, and people don't either. Out of nowhere, the ox died. Out of nowhere, its owner is still alive. One day of life is worth more than a fortune, and the price of an ox weighs less than a goose feather. If you gain a fortune and lose a penny, you can't call it a loss."
Everyone laughed at him. "By that logic, it isn't just the ox's owner who came out ahead."

He went on: "So if people hate death, they should love life. Shouldn't you enjoy being alive, every single day? Foolish people forget this pleasure and wear themselves out chasing other pleasures. They forget this treasure and risk everything for other treasures, and they're never satisfied. If you don't enjoy life while you have it, and then fear death when it comes, it doesn't add up. People don't enjoy life because they aren't afraid of death. Not that they aren't afraid of it. They just forget how close it is. And if someone says life and death don't touch him at all, then you'd have to say he has really understood."
They laughed at him even harder.

literal: 'There was a man selling an ox; the person buying said, "Tomorrow I will pay the price and take the ox."
During the night the ox died.
The person who was going to buy had a gain; the person who was going to sell had a loss', someone told.
Hearing this, a person nearby said, 'The owner of the ox did indeed have a loss, but he also had a great gain.
The reason is: that living things do not know that death is near is already so with the ox.
Unexpectedly the ox died, and unexpectedly the owner survived.
One day of life is heavier than ten thousand pieces of gold.
The price of an ox is lighter than a goose feather.
A person who gains ten thousand pieces of gold and loses one coin should not be said to have a loss', he said, and
everyone sneered and said, 'That reasoning should not be limited to the owner of the ox.'
He said again, 'So, if people hate death, they should love life.
Should one not enjoy the joy of being alive day by day?
Foolish people forget this pleasure and laboriously seek other pleasures, forget this treasure and dangerously covet other treasures, and their wishes are never fulfilled.
If, while alive, one does not enjoy life, and facing death fears death, this does not make sense.
That people all do not enjoy life is because they do not fear death.
It is not that they do not fear death; they forget that death is near.
And if someone says he is not involved in the forms of life and death, one should say he has grasped the true principle', he said, and

notes.text: {利|り} and {損|そん}: 'gain' and 'loss', the language of trade. The man nearby takes the storyteller's words and uses them for something much bigger.

notes.quote: はからざるに牛は死し、計らざるに主は存せり
notes.text: Two sentences in exactly the same shape: unexpectedly the ox died, unexpectedly the owner lived. The ox's death is the news; the owner's survival is just as surprising, but nobody notices it.
{万金|まんきん}: 'ten thousand pieces of gold', a fortune. {鵝毛|がまう}: a goose feather, a stock Chinese image for something very light. {一銭|いつせん}: one copper coin, the smallest amount of money.

notes.quote: その理は牛の主に限るべからず
notes.text: The listeners mock him: by that reasoning, everyone alive is in profit. He answers with されば, 'so then', as if they had agreed with him, and goes on.

notes.quote: 存命の喜び日々に楽しまざらむや
notes.text: む + や: a rhetorical question, 'should we not enjoy…? (We should.)'. {存命|ぞんめい}: being alive.

notes.quote: 生を楽しまざるは、死を恐れざる故なり
notes.text: A paradox, and the next sentence explains it: people do fear death, but they forget it is near, and so they never feel how lucky they are to be alive today.

notes.quote: 生死の相にあづからず
notes.text: {生死|しやうじ}: the Buddhist reading of 'life and death', also the endless cycle of birth and rebirth. あづかる: 'to be involved in'. Someone untouched by life and death has gone beyond both: that is enlightenment.
Kenkō tells us who laughed, and does not say who was right. The man nearby is never named.
